main.title: Mario Tennis: Power Tour
main.subtitle: A tennis career has a place between matches
main.summary: Mario Tennis: Power Tour is Camelot's Game Boy Advance sports role-playing game following young players through the development of a tennis career. Known in Europe as Mario Power Tennis, it combines singles and doubles matches with a story-led structure and a growing set of abilities. The handheld adventure gives the player a competitor to develop rather than only a familiar character to select. Practice and progress lead toward more demanding opponents, making the next match a test of both the player's timing and the capabilities accumulated by the tennis player taking the court.

cards.heading: A tennis career has a place between matches
cards.text: Mario Tennis: Power Tour is Camelot's Game Boy Advance sports role-playing game following young players through the development of a tennis career. Known in Europe as Mario Power Tennis, it combines singles and doubles matches with a story-led structure and a growing set of abilities. The handheld adventure gives the player a competitor to develop rather than only a familiar character to select. Practice and progress lead toward more demanding opponents, making the next match a test of both the player's timing and the capabilities accumulated by the tennis player taking the court.

cards.heading: The next return can change the rally
cards.text: Topspin, slice and other familiar strokes provide ways to alter a rally, while Power Shots introduce more dramatic offensive and defensive responses. An attacking special can make the return difficult through its force or secondary effect. A defensive one can help reach a ball or counter the extra trouble created by an opponent's power. Choosing when to use an available ability therefore matters alongside ordinary positioning. The rally remains readable as tennis, but the special actions give it additional turning points when a well-timed response can recover a seemingly lost exchange.

cards.heading: Doubles gives development another arrangement
cards.text: The campaign's sporting progress extends into doubles, where covering the court and coordinating with a partner change the demands of a point. Character development gives the continuing journey a practical result, adding another layer to the choice of stroke or special action. Power Tour follows Camelot's earlier handheld approach to Mario sports, allowing a school-style career and a more fantastic tennis world to share one structure. A particular opponent can become a milestone because reaching that match reflects the training, earlier contests and new abilities that have made the player ready to face it.

main.title: Battalion Wars
main.subtitle: Command from inside the battle
main.summary: Battalion Wars is Kuju London's action and real-time tactics game, first released for GameCube in North America on 19 September 2005.

cards.heading: Command from inside the battle
cards.text: Battalion Wars is Kuju London's action and real-time tactics game, first released for GameCube in North America on 19 September 2005. The player directly controls a soldier or vehicle while commanding the rest of a small army. Infantry, tanks and aircraft share missions across a brightly caricatured military world. The campaign begins with a conflict between rival nations before a new threat changes their alliances. Its central challenge is practical: take part in the fighting without losing track of what the other units need to accomplish.

cards.heading: Send the right unit towards the next threat
cards.text: Orders can address the whole battalion, one type of unit or an individual soldier. A group might follow the controlled character, defend a position or attack a selected target. Different weapons are suited to different opponents, so sending everyone into the same fight can waste valuable support. Switching directly into another unit changes the player's immediate role. A tank can confront armour while infantry secure a location, making the choice of who to control another part of arranging the wider force.

cards.heading: Bring the battalion home
cards.text: Mission results measure destroyed enemies, surviving allies and completion time. Moving quickly is useful only if the battalion remains strong enough to finish the objective. Cover helps protect infantry, while supplies dropped during combat can restore soldiers or repair vehicles. The game connects tactical planning to the visible condition of the force accompanying the player. A successful advance is therefore more than reaching the destination: the surviving units show how carefully the commander's decisions protected the people and equipment needed along the way.

main.title: Kingdom Under Fire: Heroes
main.subtitle: A commander belongs to the army being directed
main.summary: Kingdom Under Fire: Heroes is Blueside and Phantagram's action and real-time tactics game, first released for Xbox on 20 September 2005. Its campaigns revisit characters from The Crusaders, following events before and during that earlier story. The player commands groups of soldiers across large fantasy battles, then directly controls a hero when the commanding unit enters combat. These two perspectives are connected. The immediate fight takes place inside an army whose position and composition have already been shaped by decisions made from the broader battlefield view.

cards.heading: A commander belongs to the army being directed
cards.text: Kingdom Under Fire: Heroes is Blueside and Phantagram's action and real-time tactics game, first released for Xbox on 20 September 2005. Its campaigns revisit characters from The Crusaders, following events before and during that earlier story. The player commands groups of soldiers across large fantasy battles, then directly controls a hero when the commanding unit enters combat. These two perspectives are connected. The immediate fight takes place inside an army whose position and composition have already been shaped by decisions made from the broader battlefield view.

cards.heading: Keep the other units working while the hero fights
cards.text: Each army group contains its own soldiers, and the player's available forces include regular units and specialised support. Directing them effectively means considering more than the enemies surrounding the hero. Another group may need to move, provide assistance or confront a threat elsewhere. New elemental units, including Fire Wraiths and Earth Golems, broaden the available combinations. The player alternates between the satisfaction of landing attacks personally and the responsibility of keeping several formations useful. A powerful commander still depends on an army that reaches the right position and engages an appropriate target.

cards.heading: Seven campaigns revisit the conflict from different sides
cards.text: Ellen, Leinhart, Urukubarr, Rupert, Cirith, Morene and Walter each receive a campaign, allowing the conflict to be approached through different characters and time periods. Some stories begin five years before The Crusaders, while others take place alongside it. This structure expands the setting without abandoning the relationship between battlefield command and direct action. A Windows edition followed in 2020. Heroes is most distinctive when the two forms of control reinforce one another: the player's personal intervention matters because it takes place within a larger battle that still needs to be managed.

main.title: Drill Dozer
main.subtitle: A small pilot brings a very large drill
main.summary: Drill Dozer is Game Freak's Game Boy Advance action platformer starring Jill and the mechanical vehicle she pilots. Its drill turns in either direction, allowing the same central tool to break surfaces, engage enemies and operate objects in the surrounding levels. The cartridge contains a rumble motor that responds while drilling, giving the action a physical presence in the handheld. Rather than supplying a collection of unrelated weapons, the game builds its stages around discovering what this one machine can grip, pierce or turn as Jill searches for a route through the next obstacle.

cards.heading: A small pilot brings a very large drill
cards.text: Drill Dozer is Game Freak's Game Boy Advance action platformer starring Jill and the mechanical vehicle she pilots. Its drill turns in either direction, allowing the same central tool to break surfaces, engage enemies and operate objects in the surrounding levels. The cartridge contains a rumble motor that responds while drilling, giving the action a physical presence in the handheld. Rather than supplying a collection of unrelated weapons, the game builds its stages around discovering what this one machine can grip, pierce or turn as Jill searches for a route through the next obstacle.

cards.heading: Changing gear extends the action
cards.text: Sprockets found during a stage unlock higher gears, allowing the drill to continue longer and break more resistant blocks. Shifting at the appropriate moment keeps the action going, making sustained drilling a sequence to manage rather than simply holding a button indefinitely. The upgrades reset between stages, giving each new area its own process of building the machine back toward full capability. The player therefore reads an obstacle in relation to the gear currently available, recognising when another sprocket is needed before a promising route can actually be forced open.

cards.heading: Direction matters as much as strength
cards.text: The two shoulder buttons control opposite drilling directions, allowing the machine to interact with screws and mechanisms as well as ordinary breakable surfaces. Shops provide health improvements, drill bits and maps leading to extra stages, giving collected currency a use between expeditions. Special sections can alter how the Dozer moves, but the drill remains the reference point for solving the next problem. Its flexible use gives Jill's machine a consistent physical identity, while the rumble inside the cartridge reinforces the sensation that the same piece of equipment is working against something solid on the screen.

main.title: Sly 3: Honor Among Thieves
main.subtitle: One vault, an unlikely crew
main.summary: Sly 3: Honor Among Thieves is Sucker Punch's 2005 stealth adventure for PlayStation 2. Sly discovers the hidden Cooper family fortune and begins assembling a team capable of reaching it. Bentley and Murray return alongside new recruits, turning preparations for the final heist into a journey through a series of smaller jobs.

cards.heading: A family fortune to recover
cards.text: Sly 3: Honor Among Thieves is Sucker Punch's 2005 stealth adventure for PlayStation 2. Sly discovers the hidden Cooper family fortune and begins assembling a team capable of reaching it. Bentley and Murray return alongside new recruits, turning preparations for the final heist into a journey through a series of smaller jobs.

cards.heading: Finding a way inside
cards.text: Sly moves above the streets on rooftops and narrow ledges, looking for a route past the guards. A disguise can change how he approaches a protected area. Missions give these movements a purpose, leading the player towards an objective while the gang prepares the next stage of its plan.

cards.heading: Recruiting the right specialist
cards.text: The expanding crew brings different abilities to each operation. Bentley plans from his wheelchair, Murray supplies strength, and specialists such as the Guru introduce new ways to handle a job. Recruiting them becomes part of the adventure itself. A successful heist depends on putting several characters' skills to work.

cards.heading: Another attempt at the job
cards.text: Completed episodes can be revisited through additional challenges, asking the player to improve on an earlier job. Separate multiplayer activities offer competitive and cooperative ways to share parts of the action. The same locations and characters become material for another attempt, with a different task or another player changing the approach.

main.title: Gunstar Super Heroes
main.subtitle: Another pair of Gunstars faces the Empire
main.summary: Gunstar Super Heroes is Treasure's Game Boy Advance action game returning to the world and ideas of Gunstar Heroes through a new pair of protagonists named Red and Blue. Working with Yellow, they confront a resurrected Empire and the danger surrounding the Treasure Gems. The handheld adventure combines running and shooting with a succession of changing stage situations, using the smaller screen for a densely animated display of enemies, machinery and attacks. Its returning names connect the new journey with the earlier game while giving the pair a conflict and setting of their own to resolve.

cards.heading: Another pair of Gunstars faces the Empire
cards.text: Gunstar Super Heroes is Treasure's Game Boy Advance action game returning to the world and ideas of Gunstar Heroes through a new pair of protagonists named Red and Blue. Working with Yellow, they confront a resurrected Empire and the danger surrounding the Treasure Gems. The handheld adventure combines running and shooting with a succession of changing stage situations, using the smaller screen for a densely animated display of enemies, machinery and attacks. Its returning names connect the new journey with the earlier game while giving the pair a conflict and setting of their own to resolve.

cards.heading: Three weapons and a stored response
cards.text: Red and Blue can switch among three weapon types during play, giving the player a choice of response without needing to find and combine separate pickups. Close-range moves use button and directional combinations, adding another option when an enemy has approached beyond a comfortable shooting distance. Defeating opponents fills a supercharge meter that powers a stronger attack. The combination connects ordinary encounters with preparation for a larger threat: the player chooses a useful weapon now while gradually earning the energy that can make the next dangerous group easier to handle.

cards.heading: The chosen hero changes the account
cards.text: Story details vary with the selected character and difficulty, giving repeated journeys another narrative perspective alongside the practical challenge. Red and Blue are named after the legendary warriors of the first game, but they belong to a later conflict with its own versions of familiar figures. The connection allows recognition to sit beside change, making another playthrough more than a simple repetition of the first ending. Gunstar Super Heroes compresses that continuation into a portable action game whose shifting encounters and alternate accounts give the same short adventure several ways to be approached.

main.title: The Warriors
main.summary: The Warriors is a 2005 beat 'em up video game developed by Rockstar Toronto and published by Rockstar Games.

cards.heading: Returning to Coney Island
cards.text: The Warriors is a 2005 beat 'em up video game developed by Rockstar Toronto and published by Rockstar Games. Based on the 1979 film of the same name; it was released in October 2005 for the PlayStation 2 and Xbox, and February 2007 for the PlayStation Portable; the PSP port was developed by Rockstar Leeds. The game was re-released on the PlayStation 3 in May 2013 and PlayStation 4 in July 2016, via the PlayStation Network. Set in gritty 1970s New York City, the story follows the eponymous street gang, who are framed for the murder of a respected gang leader and must return to their home turf in Coney Island while being hunted by rival gangs and the police. The game expands on the film's plot, with the first half covering events that took place three months before the events of the film.

cards.heading: Brawling, film music and familiar voices
cards.text: The gameplay revolves around large scale brawling in 3D environments interspersed with other activities such as chase sequences. The game features songs from the film's soundtrack; however, as of 2016, some of them have been removed from the PS3 and PS4 versions, including "I Love Livin' in the City" and "In the City", due to licensing restrictions. Several cast members from the film returned to voice their characters in the game. Following its release, The Warriors received very positive reviews, with critics praising its controls, design, sound, music, and plot; many deemed the game to be a worthy adaptation of the film.

main.title: Jak X: Combat Racing
main.subtitle: A race with an antidote at the finish
main.summary: Jak X: Combat Racing is Naughty Dog's PlayStation 2 vehicular combat game, first released in North America on 18 October 2005. Jak and his companions are poisoned and forced to enter a dangerous racing championship to obtain an antidote. The spin-off turns the driving introduced in Jak 3 into the centre of a complete game. Customisable buggies compete through circuits where destroying an opponent can be as useful as passing them. The story gives the familiar cast a reason to remain in the driver's seat rather than return to a platform adventure.

cards.heading: A race with an antidote at the finish
cards.text: Jak X: Combat Racing is Naughty Dog's PlayStation 2 vehicular combat game, first released in North America on 18 October 2005. Jak and his companions are poisoned and forced to enter a dangerous racing championship to obtain an antidote. The spin-off turns the driving introduced in Jak 3 into the centre of a complete game. Customisable buggies compete through circuits where destroying an opponent can be as useful as passing them. The story gives the familiar cast a reason to remain in the driver's seat rather than return to a platform adventure.

cards.heading: Use the right colour of Eco
cards.text: Pickups connect the series' Eco to practical racing tools. Yellow supplies offensive weapons, red provides defensive options, green restores health and blue adds turbo. The player must keep a racing line while deciding how these resources can change the surrounding contest. Damage also builds a Dark Eco meter that strengthens weapons when filled. Championship events award progress through the adventure, while individual races give a reason to learn a course more closely. A clean lap remains valuable, but the next opponent can interrupt it with more than a better corner.

cards.heading: A multiplayer branch for Jak and Daxter
cards.text: Jak X became the first game in the series to include multiplayer, allowing the combat-racing rules to work between human drivers as well as through the campaign. Amy Hennig directed the project, with music by Billy Howerdel, Dean Menta and Larry Hopkins giving it a harder sound. Save data from related games could unlock additional drivers, connecting the roster to other PlayStation releases. A later PlayStation 4 edition kept the game available beside the original trilogy. It remains a substantial variation on the series, built around racing systems that had previously supported only part of its adventures.

main.title: Shadow of the Colossus
main.subtitle: The Boss Becomes the Level
main.summary: A rider and his horse cross an immense, quiet landscape in search of sixteen colossi. Climbing each moving creature turns scale, balance and observation into the central language of the adventure.

cards.heading: Climbing the creature you must defeat
cards.text: Shadow of the Colossus is Team Ico's PlayStation 2 adventure about finding and defeating sixteen immense creatures. Wander travels through the Forbidden Lands on horseback and on foot, studying each colossus before attempting to climb it. Fur, ledges and moving limbs provide routes towards a vulnerable point. The battles combine observation, climbing and combat, with the creature itself supplying much of the terrain. The North American release arrived on October 18, 2005.

cards.heading: Crossing the Forbidden Lands
cards.text: Plains, canyons, lakes and ruins separate the encounters. On Agro's back, the player crosses distances visible far ahead, with time to take in the landscape between fights. Fumito Ueda described the depth of field as an important consideration in both Ico and Shadow of the Colossus. Here it allows a distant destination to remain visible during the journey. The quiet travel gives each new colossus a different kind of entrance after the intensity of the previous battle.

cards.heading: Finding a secure grip
cards.text: A grip meter limits how long Wander can hold on. A colossus shakes, changes its posture and moves the surface beneath him, so reaching a weak point involves finding a secure position as well as a route. Pauses allow him to recover his grip before attempting the next climb. The team worked on animation, control and collisions together to make these movements convincing: the player needs to feel both Wander's effort and the creature's capacity to dislodge him.

cards.heading: Travelling with Agro
cards.text: Agro has its own inertia and responds to the terrain, requiring the player to guide a moving animal. Calling the horse and relying on it for long journeys establish a companionship through repeated actions. Ueda described Wander and Agro as having a strong bond before the story begins. Their routine gives that relationship a place in play, from crossing open ground together to the contrast of Wander continuing alone.

cards.heading: The aftermath of a victory
cards.text: Defeating a colossus advances Wander's quest, but the aftermath gives the player time to consider what has happened. The creature falls, the music changes and Wander's body absorbs visible consequences. Repeating these encounters makes the cost of his progress increasingly apparent. Creators recalling the game for PlayStation remembered the discomfort of their first victory, a response prompted by the same action that carries the story forward.

cards.heading: Moving terrain on PlayStation 2
cards.text: The colossi require animation, collision, camera and character control to cooperate on a large scale. Wander must be able to run over a sloping back, grip its fur and remain visible as the creature moves. The team's technical postmortem describes the work behind these encounters. The original PlayStation 2 version also shows the strain through its frame-rate limits. Its most ambitious technical problem was making a human character's precarious movement convincing on a much larger moving body.

cards.heading: Wander and Mono
cards.text: Wander enters the isolated region seeking the power to revive Mono. His task is to locate and destroy sixteen colossi scattered across the land. Searching on horseback and approaching each creature on foot make that objective the centre of the adventure. The restricted cast and repeated task leave room for the player to reflect on Wander's determination and on the consequences that follow each encounter.

cards.heading: From NICO to a solitary journey
cards.text: The game was directed by Fumito Ueda and developed at Sony Computer Entertainment's International Production Studio 1, also known as Team Ico, the same development team responsible for the acclaimed PlayStation 2 title Ico, to which the game is considered a spiritual successor. Сonceived as an online multiplayer game titled NICO directly after Ico's completion, Shadow of the Colossus underwent a lengthy production cycle during which it was redeveloped as a single-player title. The team sought to create an outstanding interactive experience by including a distinct visual design, an unorthodox gameplay template, and non-player characters with sophisticated artificial intelligence such as the colossi and Wander's horse, Agro.

cards.heading: Reception, remaster and remake
cards.text: Cited as an influential title in the video game industry and one of the best video games of all time, Shadow of the Colossus is often regarded as an important example of video games as art due to its minimalist landscape designs, immersive gameplay, and emotional weight of the player character's journey. It received wide critical acclaim by the media and was met with strong sales compared to Ico, due in part to a larger marketing campaign. The game won several awards for its audio, design, and overall quality. A remastered version for the PlayStation 3 was released alongside Ico as The Ico & Shadow of the Colossus Collection in September 2011, developed by Bluepoint Games, who later developed a remake of the game in high definition for the PlayStation 4 in 2018.

main.title: F.E.A.R.
main.summary: F.E.A.R. combines a first-person shooter with psychological horror. Monolith’s original Windows game places tactical firefights and unsettling supernatural encounters in the same space.

cards.heading: Slow-motion action and psychological horror
cards.text: F.E.A.R. is Monolith Productions' 2005 first-person shooter combining military action with psychological horror. Released for Windows by Vivendi Universal Games in October, it follows a specialist unit investigating supernatural events. Point Man's quick reactions support a slow-motion combat ability, while disturbing visions interrupt the fighting. Day 1 Studios later brought the game to Xbox 360 in 2006 and PlayStation 3 in 2007. TimeGate developed the standalone expansions Extraction Point and Perseus Mandate.

cards.heading: Point Man enters the compound
cards.text: A paramilitary force takes over an aerospace compound, and the first military response ends in a mysterious massacre. The F.E.A.R. unit is sent to investigate and eliminate the intruders. Playing its newest recruit, Point Man, the player moves between firefights and paranormal manifestations involving a girl in red. His unusually quick reactions give the combat its distinctive pace, while his past forms part of the mystery.

cards.heading: Enemies who fight as a team
cards.text: Monolith combined influences from Japanese horror with the spectacle of an action film. Reflex time slows combat, making the effects of bullets, particles and damage to the surroundings more visible. Enemy behaviour gives these fights much of their variety: soldiers can flank the player, provide suppressive fire for one another and retreat under pressure. Their ability to respond as a group makes a firefight feel different from an exchange with isolated targets.

cards.heading: Reception and console versions
cards.text: Upon its initial Windows release, F.E.A.R. was very well received, with the AI garnering particular praise. Critics also lauded the graphics, atmosphere, sound design, music, and combat mechanics. Common points of criticism were a lack of enemy variety, a weak plot, and repetitive level design. The Xbox 360 version was also well received, but the PlayStation 3 version met with mixed reviews, with many critics unimpressed with the port's technical issues and graphical inferiority. It was a commercial success, selling over three million units worldwide across all three systems.
